title: Adaptive prefill admission controller with kernel cost hints and tenant crediting
creator: Priya Kapoor
description: Design and implement an adaptive admission controller for prefill/decode that uses lightweight kernel cost hints and attention-density signals to decide: (1) whether to split a request's work into micro-phases, (2) when to opportunistically bundle micro-slices for throughput, and (3) how to debit tenant credits for fair access. Goal is to reduce p95 tail latency regressions under mixed workloads while recovering utilization for throughput workloads without inducing tenant starvation.
background: Current prefill/decode scheduler operates with coarse-grained phase splitting heuristics that do not account for per-request kernel cost or attention sparsity. This leads to either: (a) conservative splitting that increases latency for latency-sensitive tenants, or (b) aggressive batching that damages fairness for small high-priority requests. We observed p95 spikes during multi-tenant microburst traces (see dashboard link). Kernel selection (attention-optimized vs generic kernels) has different throughput/latency curves and should influence admission decisions.
goals: Reduce p95 latency for latency-tier tenants by >= 20% on synthetic multi-tenant microbursts
Maintain or improve average GPU utilization for throughput workloads (tokens/sec) within 5% of baseline
Prevent starvation: 99.9% of high-priority requests must start service within their budgeted latency window
Provide observability hooks for per-tenant credit balance, kernel choice, and micro-slice decisions
acceptance_criteria: Admission controller produces stable per-tenant credit debits and logs decisions to tracing system
A/B experiment comparing new controller vs baseline shows p95 latency reduction >= 20% for latency tenants under mixed load
No more than 0.1% of requests are delayed beyond configured tenant budget in sustained 30-minute tests
PRs merged for runtime, routing, and console visualization; integration tests passing in CI and staging
Runbook updated with steps to toggle controller feature flag and emergency fallback to legacy scheduler
design_decisions: Use a two-stage admission model: fast path lightweight estimator (kernel-cost hint + attention-density bucket) followed by scheduler decision that may split into micro-phases
Kernel-cost hints are estimated at request admission using model metadata (architecture, token counts) plus a tiny profiling table built from prior runs per model-version and sequence-length bucket
Attention-density signal computed from prefill tokens heuristics (e.g., presence of dense attention patterns or known sparsity flags) to select attention-optimized kernels where beneficial
Tenant credits operate as soft budgets with leaky-bucket refill; high-priority tenants have higher refill rates and emergency headroom to avoid starvation
Fairness arbitration uses a decay-weighted recent-usage metric to demote opportunistic batching for tenants near zero credit
Fallback demotion: when kernel contention or capacity strain detected, automatically switch to a demoted path that reduces micro-slice bundling and prioritizes earliest-deadline requests
tradeoffs_and_risks: Accuracy of kernel-cost hints: misestimates can either cause unnecessary splitting (higher overhead) or too-large batches (latency regression). Mitigation: continuous online calibration table and conservative smoothing

Complexity in tenant credit tuning: overly aggressive crediting reduces utilization; too strict crediting causes unhappy customers. Mitigation: staged rollout with telemetry-driven tuning and canary tenants
Interaction with quantized kernels: some quantized kernels may change cost model; we must tag cost hints with quantization profile to avoid bad routing
Observability surface increases: more metrics/traces required which add ingestion cost. We'll sample 10% of decisions at high fidelity and aggregate for dashboards
implementation_notes: Runtime changes: admission controller component inside router service that consumes model version metadata and attention hints from request pre-parsing
Scheduler changes: extend existing phase splitter to accept a 'suggested-split' object with micro-slice sizes and kernel preference tags
Kernel probe: small periodic probes (one probe per model-version per node per 10 minutes) to refresh cost table; probes logged to perf DB
Config flags: experimental.adaptive_prefill_admission (boolean), admission.credit_policy (json-like stringified config), admission.kernel_probe_interval_seconds
Console: new panel under Console -> Runtime -> Scheduling showing per-tenant credit balances, split rates, kernel-choice histogram
Integration with Optimize: suggestion engine will consume historical logs to propose credit parameters and split thresholds per workload
testing_plan: Unit tests for admission decision logic and credit accounting
Staging integration tests with mixed workload generator: latency-heavy-tenant + background-throughput-tenant traces
Chaos tests: kill a serving node during micro-slice execution to validate rollback semantics and idempotency
Perf bench: run multi-tenant microburst trace (trace_id: mtb-2026-02) measuring p50/p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec across baseline vs new controller
A/B canary: roll out to 5% of hosts, monitor SLOs and customer-facing errors for 48 hours before wider rollout
metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency for prefill and decode stages
fairness_score (Gini-like metric on request start latency across tenants)
rollout_plan: Feature gated behind experimental.adaptive_prefill_admission; default off
Deploy admission controller binary to staging with mock cost table; validate end-to-end in staging (2 days)
Canary deploy to 5% hosts for 48h; run automated canary checks (latency SLOs, error rates, fairness metrics)
If canary green, expand to 25% for one week with active tuning of credit parameters
Full cluster roll (100%) after two successful weeks or earlier rollback if p99 latency increases > 10% for latency tenants
Provide quick rollback: flip experimental.adaptive_prefill_admission to false to revert to legacy scheduler
